items.title: Germany's Hospitals Prepare for War and Mass Casualties as Russia Threat Looms
body: At first glance, the hospital in the southwestern German city of Ulm looks much like any other. Patients sit in reception areas waiting to be called, doctors roam the halls looking at reports or their phones. Only the uniformed soldiers among the staff hint at military ties. Yet many meters beneath its busy wards lies a Cold War-era bunker that has suddenly become relevant again.

The underground medical facility was completed in 1979 amid the standoff between Moscow and the West. It was designed to let doctors continue treating injured soldiers in the event of a nuclear strike, and can house up to 2,000 people for 90 days. For the better part of three decades, the labyrinthine facility sat dormant. Now, the German military is considering reviving it.

Across the country, government bodies are surveying Germany’s healthcare systems and infrastructure to see how — or if — they would stand up in a defense scenario. Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Germany has seen a surge in hybrid attacks, such as an attempted strike at an airport by an explosive-laden drone in Leipzig last month and various cyberattacks targeting hospitals. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has warned that Russia may be in a position to attack NATO territory by 2029. If that were to happen, Germany would be obligated to come to the alliance’s defense, and given its position in the heart of Europe, the country would likely become a key transit hub for soldiers — and a destination for their medical treatment.
Read: Germany Blames Russia for Attempted Drone Attack, Expects More

In a report that gamed out potential scenarios should Russia invade NATO territory, the Bundeswehr calculated that as many as 1,000 wounded soldiers could arrive in Germany each day. As the country’s five military hospitals would quickly reach capacity — and the law requires that civilian hospitals help during wartime — the system would likely come under unprecedented strain, and could be forced to triage soldier and civilian care.

That, in turn, has focused attention on facilities like Ulm, which is a rare example of a military medical bunker in good enough shape to be brought back into use. But doing so would require spending millions of euros to modernize its decades-old ventilation and power systems, and would just be a drop in the bucket compared with what’s needed overall.

“Is our healthcare system prepared for this? The only answer is: No,” said Benedikt Friemert, chief medical director and commander of the Military Hospital hospital in Ulm. “What lies ahead of us is a marathon.”

Finding enough hospital beds is just part of the challenge. Germany’s leaders also need to reinforce medical supply chains and better coordinate the military and civilian hospital systems. Training is another concern: only a few hundred doctors in Germany are estimated to have experience handling war-related injuries. To improve these numbers, the Bundeswehr and the German Trauma Society DGU offer courses for civilian surgeons on treating mass-casualty events and wartime injuries.

When that collaboration was formalized in 2017, the world was very different, recalled Sascha Flohé, secretary general of DGU. “Back then, we still thought we were living in a safe world, apart from Islamist terrorism,” he said. “Nobody believed the security situation would change completely, or that we would be talking about collective-defense scenarios.” Now, demand is high, with some state governments booking out full weeks of classes, and spots are hard to come by. The most intensive programs, which utilize cadavers and anesthetized pigs, are only able to train between 50 and 100 surgeons a year.

Should war break out, the Bundeswehr’s medical forces would treat injured soldiers at the frontline before transporting them to Germany, where state authorities would send them on to civilian hospitals. That strategy was tested in March, when the military conducted its largest medical exercise in decades, simulating an attack on Lithuania and moving soldiers to hospitals in Berlin and parts of Brandenburg. The exercise went smoothly, Flohé said, but more practice is needed to ensure that the two systems can communicate effectively during an emergency.

The Health Security Act, which was expected to reach parliament this fall, is intended to do this by creating a real-time overview of beds, medicines and staff with war-relevant skills. But for now, it’s all piecemeal, making it difficult to know where specialists are available or if doctors and nurses who also volunteer for aid organizations or serve as reservists are being properly accounted for.

“At the moment we have these islands, the hospitals,” said Maria-Lena Weiss, a lawmaker with the Christian Democratic Union and a member of the Bundestag’s health committee. “Now it’s about connecting them to the overall system.”

Without government guidance, some companies have started to do their own calculations. Biotech company CSL found that as many as 20% of its employees in some areas could be called away as reservists or volunteers. Annegret Wittich-Höffer, the company’s head of Germany, Austria and Switzerland, also noted that truck drivers, many of whom come from Eastern Europe, could be called up by their home countries. The company is also figuring out how to continue producing critical medicines if demand suddenly soars. To make a drug used in trauma surgeries, CSL must first collect and process plasma donations. That, however, can take up to a year and the limited shelf-life of the finished products make it difficult to create strategic reserves.

“Without blood-clotting factors, things get really tight,” said Wittich-Höffer. Should wounded soldiers start coming into Germany for care at the scale that the Bundeswehr has laid out, she said, “nobody will be prepared — neither we nor our competitors.”

Hospitals, especially larger ones, are also seeking advice on resilience and emergency planning, said Michael Ey, a partner at PwC who specializes in healthcare. In addition to weighing physical protections such as bullet-resistant glass and protective barriers against drones, some are assessing how long medicines and surgical supplies would last in a crisis. “Our economy has largely been built around just-in-time supply chains. That may be good for efficiency and minimizing tied-up capital, but that’s not how resilience is built,” Ey said, arguing Germany needs decentralized stockpiles of masks, medicines and vaccines stored across multiple locations.

Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine was a real-world example of how medical systems adapt to war. Kateryna Bielka, an anesthesiologist and professor in Kyiv, recalls how staff at her hospital improvised, moving patients to lower floors that were supposedly safer, barricading windows to protect against flying glass during air strikes and converting underground spaces such as changing or technical rooms into treatment areas. When Russia began attacking energy infrastructure, hospitals began diversifying their electricity sources, bringing in generators and solar panels. One of the biggest challenges throughout, she said, was dealing with uncertainty: “the high level of stress, lack of information, lack of understanding.”

Just across from the Military Hospital, the Ulm University Hospital is also preparing for worst-case scenarios. It has a dedicated crisis and resilience team that stages terror drills and is currently looking into whether the building’s underground parking garage could be converted into a long-term emergency shelter in the event of an attack.

Udo Kaisers, the university hospital’s chief medical officer, said that many German buildings were constructed at a time when resilience and crisis preparedness weren’t top priorities. And financing and grants generally cover only the most cost-effective construction or renovation measures, not the most durable ones.

He also worries about vulnerabilities in the medical supply chain. Germany, like much of Europe, is dependent on China for many critical ingredients needed in antibiotics and painkillers. While his hospital is increasing stocks of some essential drugs, budgetary concerns make this complicated. Hospitals in Germany are advised to stock only six weeks of intensive-care medicines.

There is broad political support for updating the country’s legal framework in order to keep the healthcare system functioning in a defense or wartime scenario. The previous government was working on this, but failed to complete it before collapsing in 2024. The current coalition was expected to present a draft of the Health Security Act this summer, but postponed it to fall — and it’s unclear whether that target will be reached.
Despite all the uncertainty, keeping hospitals functioning during turbulent times is at the heart of everything, said Kaisers.

“The healthcare system is central to the functioning of society,” he said. “Social cohesion, and ultimately also public morale, depend significantly on whether we can uphold the promise of healthcare for people.”

items.title: Europe's New Stocks Tape Needs to Go Deeper, Industry Groups Say
body: A long-awaited feed of data on European stocks finally went live this week, but groups representing banks, investors and traders say it doesn’t go far enough.

Five lobby groups are calling on the European Union to increase the depth of the data to include the location stock quotes come from, in a joint statement on Wednesday. They say it would allow investors to make more informed decisions and increase the attractiveness of Europe’s markets.

It comes as Brussels is working through a package of wide-ranging financial reforms known as the Market Integration and Supervision Package, or MISP, that aims to streamline the region’s capital markets. The European Commission’s original MISP proposals include upgrades to the so-called consolidated tape, but the final version still has to be agreed with the European Parliament, as well as EU member states.
Read More: Europe’s Fractured Stock Market Finally Gets a Single Data Feed

“A truly high-quality tape would provide a single view of trading and liquidity across EU markets,” the associations, including the European Banking Federation and European Fund and Asset Management Association, wrote. “By making dispersed liquidity more visible, it supports informed execution decisions and will make European markets more accessible and attractive to global investors.”

Since Monday, equity investors can access a data feed amalgamating activity on the region’s myriad bourses and trading venues. The feed provides the best bid and ask prices in the region without disclosing the venue they originated from. Instead, traders can see more granular data after a transaction has taken place.

In the letter, the groups, which also include the Association for Financial Markets in Europe, the European Principal Traders Association and the Managed Funds Association, said the debate around the legislation should move away from prescribing where trades should take place and instead make liquidity more visible.

The groups are at odds with Europe’s stock exchanges, which point to the rise of alternative trading venues and systemic internalizers, banks that match client orders through their books, for the slump in new listings and the perception that the region is less liquid than the US.
The associations also called on Brussels to limit the fees market participants pay exchanges to access their data and streamline clearing and settlement of securities such as stocks and bonds.

items.title: Bitcoin Under Renewed Pressure as Looming Fed Hike Adds to Woes
body: Cryptocurrencies face renewed pressure after the US failed to advance a key regulatory bill, bruising industry sentiment just ahead of a potential interest-rate hike from the Federal Reserve.

Bitcoin, which fell 4% in US trading, declined further in Asia Wednesday before stabilizing at around $75,700 at 11:50 a.m. in Singapore. The broader cryptocurrency market was also weaker in early Asia trading after steep declines in the US.

Investors had been looking to the Clarity Act — a crypto market structure bill that was under consideration for over a year — to help the market break out of an 11-month malaise, even as the bill was seen as having a low chance of progressing in the Senate this week amid political wrangling. Now inflation fears and soaring US bond yields are expected to push Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh to raise rates Wednesday, which could further damp demand for risk assets like Bitcoin.

The failure to progress Clarity “adds additional headwinds in the short term for a move up in Bitcoin,” said Pratik Kala, a portfolio manager at digital-asset hedge fund Apollo Crypto. “Until investors gain more certainty on the path of rates globally, risk assets would remain under pressure,” he added.
Over $560 million in bullish bets on cryptocurrencies were unwound in the last 24 hours, according to Coinglass data.

However, positioning in Bitcoin showed some resilience. There are more bets on the original cryptocurrency to rise than to fall, according to data on Deribit. Roughly $1.7 billion in calls were held at the $80,000 level across all maturities, the data show.
Read more: Crypto’s Push Into Wall Street Suffers Setback After Bill Fails

Industry executives were quick to express frustration over the failed Senate vote on Tuesday, as it was meant to lend legitimacy to crypto as it further integrated into Wall Street. In posts on X, Ripple Labs Chief Executive Officer Brad Garlinghouse called for a post-mortem looking at why the bill failed, while Coinbase Inc. CEO Brian Armstrong said the industry could no longer wait on Congress.

Both pointed to the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission as being able to offer a clear regulatory framework in the absence of legislation. However, agency rules could prove easier for a future administration to change.

“This points to the larger challenge ahead,” said Samson Leo, chief legal officer at the Singapore-based stablecoin issuer StraitsX. “The longer major markets operate without clear and compatible frameworks, the harder it becomes to address fragmentation.”
But the immediate focus is now on the Fed, with markets pricing a better than 90% chance of a 25 basis-point hike, swaps data show.

“Market turmoil is to be expected across all asset classes if Warsh fails to hike rates,” said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. She added that inflation concerns could revive the debasement trade, which is positive for Bitcoin, but “bond yields mayhem and general market volatility will probably take it down first before it goes up.”

items.title: Hong Kong Sets Five-Year Tech Goals, Expands Baby Bonus
body: Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee set out plans to almost double the city’s spending on innovation in coming years and offered greater financial support for new parents, as his government seeks to build new growth engines growth and arrest a decline in births.

The innovation target was announced Wednesday as Lee unveiled Hong Kong’s first five-year development plan. The city will strive to make total domestic expenditure on innovation activities account for 3% of gross domestic product after 2030, up from 1.63% in 2024.

“We will closely align with our country’s strategic technology areas,” Lee said in a speech, naming life and health technology, artificial intelligence and robotics, and microelectronics among focus areas. China’s research and development expenditure accounted for 2.8% of GDP last year.
Lee followed the five-year plan with his annual policy address, which set out measures for putting the longer-term blueprint into effect and offered more immediate support to households.

The government will extend the one-time newborn baby bonus of HK$20,000 ($2,550) for three years through October 2029 and raise the payment for second and subsequent children to HK$30,000. Homebuyers who buy an apartment within one year before or two years after the birth of a child will also receive a HK$20,000 reduction in stamp duty. The existing newborn bonus was first announced in the 2023 policy speech for an initial three-year period.

Lee emphasized national security in the the policy address, calling it a “never-ending process” that must not be overlooked in the pursuit of development. The government will continue to strengthen the legal system and enforcement mechanisms for safeguarding national security. To promote patriotic education, the city will establish a museum to showcase China’s achievements in areas such as technology, sports and culture.

The emphasis continues a central theme of the Hong Kong government since Beijing imposed a National Security Law in 2020 that has silenced dissent and led to the imprisonment of dozens of critics, including former media mogul Jimmy Lai. Lee, a former security chief, said the enforcement of security laws has provided the stability and predictability needed for economic growth, describing the former British colony as a “safe harbor” for development.

The new five-year plan calls for AI to become a core industry for Hong Kong and be applied more widely across finance, trade, logistics, professional services and healthcare. The government will expand computing infrastructure through a Sandy Ridge data facility due to start operating by 2029 and review legislation to support wider AI use.

A key part of Lee’s technology drive is the Northern Metropolis project bordering the mainland city of Shenzhen. That development is intended to provide land, infrastructure and talent for tech and emerging industries. He set a binding goal of increasing “spade-ready sites” — plots that can be readily used for development — to 900 hectares by 2031 from 120 this year.

The Hang Seng Property Index advanced as Lee highlighted cross-border initiatives and progress on the future tech hub. Developers with ample liquidity stood out, with Longfor Group, Hang Lung Properties and Sun Hung Kai Properties among the biggest gainers.

The longer-term plan also seeks to enhance Hong Kong’s traditional roles as a center for finance and trade. The government plans to expand offshore yuan products, promote the currency’s use in settling public expenditure and develop a commodity-trading ecosystem with gold as an entry point.

Hong Kong will seek to attract more global companies and talent, targeting annual growth of 4% to 5% in the number of businesses with parent companies located outside the city. Three university towns planned for the Northern Metropolis will combine education, research and industry, with student housing and other services designed to attract international talent.
Lee did not set a hard target for GDP growth, saying only that the economy should expand at a pace “within a reasonable range” through 2030.

The innovation goal aligns Hong Kong with China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, which puts technological self-reliance at the center of the country’s strategy. Beijing is seeking breakthroughs in fields including advanced chips, quantum computing and robotics as competition with the US intensifies and American export controls expose China’s dependence on foreign technology.

Artificial intelligence is a particular focus. China’s national plan calls for AI to be deployed across the economy, including in manufacturing and other industries, as Beijing seeks to raise productivity and compete with the US for leadership in the technology.

items.title: State-Backed China Water Environment Defaults on Offshore Loan
body: China Water Environment Group, one of the nation’s largest sewage treatment firms, failed to repay an offshore loan recently, people familiar with the matter said, in the latest default by a state-backed company.

The Beijing-based firm, partially owned by the State Development and Investment Corp., missed payment on $61 million in outstanding principal due in late August after creditors rejected its request to extend the loan for a few months, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

It’s unclear why China Water Environment Group asked to delay the payment. But some other Chinese public-sector enterprises have faced mounting financial stress in recent years, as the amount of money owed to them from business partners including local governments has remained elevated amid broader economic challenges.

China Water Environment, which serves about 45 million people across 22 provincial-level regions and has worked on some key national environmental initiatives, isn’t SDIC’s only subsidiary to face debt problems. Earlier this year, a unit of SDIC Commodities Co., a metals trader controlled by the state firm, was ordered to liquidate by a Hong Kong court after the unit failed to repay some offshore debt.

The water company’s default was flagged by the agent bank to lenders on another one of its loans—a $130 million borrowing due 2028, the people added. Those creditors were asked if they wanted to take actions to trigger a cross-default clause, according to the people. It wasn’t clear if those lenders had any response.
China Water Environment and SDIC didn’t respond to requests seeking comment.
In 2018, SDIC acquired a 43% stake in the company and became the single largest shareholder, according to a public filing in 2022.

items.title: Indonesia Cuts Benchmark Ore Prices in Relief for Nickel Plants
body: Indonesia slashed benchmark prices for lower-grade nickel ore, providing relief for local processors suffering from cost pressures due to the US-Iran war.

The formula used to calculate the Mineral Benchmark Price, or HPM, has been changed to reduce the minimum price payable for low-grade ore, according to a ministerial regulation that came into effect on Friday. At the new level, the cost of 1.2% nickel ore will be almost halved, according to calculations by Bloomberg.

The change will benefit high pressure acid leach plants, which process low-grade nickel ore into a chemical that’s used by the electric vehicle battery sector. HPALs have already been dealing with a spike in the price of key reagent sulfur due to the Middle East war, forcing some to weigh joint cuts to production.

Significant new HPAL capacity is due to ramp up this year and next, potentially putting more pressure on nickel prices that fell to the lowest level this year on Wednesday. The product they make, known as mixed hydroxide precipitate, can also be converted into pure nickel metal that can be stored in London Metal Exchange warehouses.

The benchmark change is a u-turn for Indonesia’s energy and mineral resources ministry, which altered the formula as recently as April. The gauge is used to calculate royalties paid by miners and processors on their output, and the government has sought additional revenue to cover the costs of President Prabowo Subianto’s flagship policies.

items.title: Chanel Designer Matthieu Blazy Outpaces Gucci, Dior
body: A year ago, new designers at Chanel, Dior and Gucci gave top-end customers a glimpse of their creative visions.

Installed as part of the great luxury reset, in which more than a dozen brands changed designers, the major fashion houses’ fresh faces aimed to end the complacency of the previous five years, when labels produced not only expensive bags, shoes and clothes, but boring ones, too.

With shares in Louis Vuitton and Dior owner  LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE at their lowest since 2020, and Kering SA’s Gucci yet to stage a comeback, big bling’s outfit change is still a work in progress. More effort is needed to inject excitement into mainstream luxury brands, in the way that niche labels such as Phoebe Philo appear to be doing. At the same time, they must reconnect with customers who can’t pay $4,000 for a suit, but still want a slice of something luxurious.

From the runways to resale, Chanel has been the clear standout. Designer Matthieu Blazy caused a frenzy when the first deliveries of his lines arrived in stores in March. Chanel’s sales rose 16% in the first half of this year excluding currency movements. By comparison, LVMH’s fashion and leather goods sales fell 1% in the same period.

Blazy was able to make such a splash because Chanel didn’t rush to appoint a big name after the death of Karl Lagerfeld in 2019. Not only was this respectful, but it allowed enough time to pass between the Lagerfeld and Blazy eras. The new designer was also given a long lead time: After being appointed in late 2024, he didn’t show his first collection until October 2025.

As Chanel is privately owned by brothers Alain and Gerard Wertheimer, it could afford to be patient. The strategy worked, creating — and then unleashing — pent-up demand for Blazy’s oversized bags, tweed jackets and square-toed shoes. Chanel also cleverly introduced new purses priced below its most expensive classics, which helped even top-end customers feel they were getting more value for money.

Listed rivals don’t have the same freedom. Jonathan Anderson officially took the reins at Dior in spring 2025 and delivered his first menswear collection just a few months later. While Dior may be behind Chanel, Anderson’s products are finding an audience. Dior’s second-quarter revenue growth outpaced the average for the fashion and leather goods division, which eked out a 1% gain, LVMH said.

I’m also optimistic about Michael Rider at Dior’s sister brand Celine. The American designer worked with Philo at Celine before leading the women’s division at Polo Ralph Lauren, grounding him not only in high fashion, but in wearable styles.

New names at other houses including LVMH’s Fendi and Kering’s Balenciaga have yet to make a splash. But the biggest brand still finding its way is Gucci. Despite delving into the archives, creative director Demna Gvasalia has yet come up with his own, compelling identity.

Demna’s debut a year ago was promising. The cast of typical Italian characters portrayed in the brand’s “La Famiglia” collection and accompanying advertising campaign sent the message that everyone was welcome at the house. But his first runway show in February went darker, narrowing prospective purchasers to the very young and very skinny. While Gucci’s second quarter sales were better than expected, they are still going in the wrong direction.
We are now at the point where the class of 2024 and 2025 are are in their sophomore years, and many of their products are in stores.

For Chanel, the task is to keep wowing its customers — both with Blazy’s creations and its winning combination of style and price in handbags. At Dior, Anderson needs to more clearly articulate what makes the brand special, and why customers should buy it rather than Chanel. As LVMH’s second biggest fashion division, Dior may have to do some heavy lifting: Louis Vuitton’s Chinese sales have been hurt by a fight with a local teamaker that sparked a patriotic backlash, Bloomberg News reported.
For all of these labels, consistency is key. Even the wealthy want items that can last more than one season.

Demna has the most to prove. Broadening customer appeal is imperative. His blockbuster show in New York’s Times Square in May portrayed the city’s archetypes, reminiscent of the La Famiglia campaign. But returning more wholeheartedly to different personas — and multiple facets of the brand — in Milan next week would be wise.

If Demna can’t reignite the spark at Gucci, it will have to rely on cutting prices, which it has already done to some extent. This has helped it to reach so-called aspirational consumers, particularly in the US. But releasing too many bags with lower price tags risks cheapening the brand, from which it will be hard to recover.

Fixing Gucci is already Kering CEO Luca de Meo’s number one priority. It may be about to become even more crucial: The fashion press is speculating that Anthony Vaccarello, creative director of Saint Laurent for the past decade, is poised to leave, to be succeeded by Chloe’s Chemena Kamali. Saint Laurent has been one of Kering’s most stable brands, so further upheaval would be unhelpful.

But success or failure transcends brand boundaries. Collectively, the industry’s primary task is to make luxury matter again. Despite the unprecedented round of musical sewing machines, relevance and sales growth across much of the sector remain some way off.

items.title: Japan's Jera Looks to Pivot LNG Buying Muscle Into Global Sales
body: Jera Co., one of the world’s biggest liquefied natural gas buyers, is seeking to broaden long-term exports of the fuel as a way to expand its global presence and offload excess supply.

Japan’s largest power producer – which imports LNG primarily for domestic consumption – is seeking to “identify additional markets where we can sell,” said Irtiza Sayyed, chief executive officer of Jera Global Energy Solutions, which oversees the company’s long-term LNG business.

“We have a renewed focus in that area,” Sayyed said in an interview on the sidelines of the Gastech conference in Bangkok, adding that Jera GES had opened talks with potential buyers and was considering prospective markets around the world.

Many Asian countries in particular are seeking alternative supplies of LNG as the ongoing war in the Middle East disrupts flows of the super-chilled fuel through the Strait of Hormuz, which used to handle a fifth of global shipments. Buyers are seeking to reduce risk by securing contracts with exporters outside the Persian Gulf.
Read More: Thailand’s PTT Seeks LNG Deals in US Gulf to Widen Supply Base

Jera GES was launched in July to manage the company’s long-term LNG portfolio, including contracts that last 10 years or longer. Locking in overseas buyers for years will allow Jera to have a demand outlet when consumption is lower in Japan, or if there is excess supply.

The Japanese company announced its first long-term export supply deal late last year, agreeing to deliver four cargoes annually over the next decade to privately owned Indian utility Torrent Power Ltd. The shipments – totaling around 270,000 tons a year – are due to begin in 2027.

In a separate interview Tuesday, Jera Co.’s chairman and global chief executive officer, Yukio Kani, said the company had “extra cargoes” available after an unusually cool summer in Tokyo. These could be diverted to help other Asian countries, he said, adding that Jera had secured “almost everything” it needs for the winter.
Read More: Japan’s Jera Sees LNG Spot Prices Rising as Winter Approaches

Jera GES will also seek to charter additional LNG carriers in the later part of the decade as its exposure to the US Gulf Coast increases, Sayyed said. By around 2030, the company expects to procure about 30% of its LNG on a long-term basis from the region, compared with 10% currently.

items.title: Indian Bonds Feel the Heat From Global Yield Surge
body: Good morning... I’m Samie Modak in Mumbai, with bond markets continuing to command global investors’ attention.The 10-year US Treasury yield climbed to the highest in almost two decades on Tuesday, the latest milestone in a bruising bond selloff ahead of the Federal Reserve’s rate decision. Markets are pricing in a more-than-90% chance of a hike, which would be the first since 2023.The decision is set to have repercussions for Indian bonds as well, which have just witnessed heavy outflows from foreign investors, as we write below.In stocks, the anchor book for the National Stock Exchange of India’s much-awaited IPO opens on Wednesday, ahead of the main offering later this week. The benchmark NSE Nifty 50 Index slid to a five-month low on Tuesday, with gauges of small-cap and mid-cap shares falling even harder as elevated crude prices and weak global markets dented risk appetite. Shares of digital payment firms, including Paytm and MobiKwik, will be in focus after the government announced a fee on merchant transactions.Meanwhile, there was some good news on the macro front. India’s trade deficit in August narrowed more than economists expected on robust export growth.
In today’s newsletter, we cover:

Foreign investors sold 47.3 billion rupees ($490 million) of index-eligible government bonds on Friday, their biggest single-day exit since April 2025 and the second-largest in at least three years, according to Clearing Corp. of India data compiled by Bloomberg. The outflow came as the yield gap between domestic bonds and US Treasuries shrank to the smallest in over two decades, and before the broad market selloff witnessed on Tuesday in response to the RBI’s plan to sell sovereign notes to drain excess cash from lenders. As US yields keep moving higher and bets grow on a Fed rate hike, pressure is building on other central banks, including the Reserve Bank of India, to be more aggressive in tightening monetary policy.
Dr Reddy’s leads domestic pharma growth: I-Sec

India’s pharma market kept up a healthy pace in August, growing 13% from a year earlier to 248 billion rupees, according to ICICI Securities. Growth was strongest in chronic treatments, up 16%, while acute therapies rose 11%. Oncology, diabetes and cardiac drugs led the gains, while respiratory and anti-infective medicines grew more slowly. Volumes were up just 0.6%, suggesting much of the market growth is still coming from price increases and new product launches. Among the top 20 companies, Dr Reddy’s grew the fastest at about 22%, followed by Ajanta, Glenmark, Mankind, Zydus and Torrent. GLP-1 sales were broadly steady at 2.8 billion rupees, with generic semaglutide now outselling four innovator brands.
Momentum trade delaying rebound in large-caps: Kotak

Kotak says several large-cap stocks are now trading well below what it sees as fair value, a shift from the recent market trend. But that doesn’t mean they will rebound quickly. The brokerage says momentum-driven investing has made valuations less important, with investors focusing more on short-term news and treating a few quarters of earnings as if they will last indefinitely. Instead of debating whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its underlying value, many investors are positioning around the next expected trigger. That can leave fundamentally attractive stocks stuck in the “value” bucket for longer than usual, Kotak said.
Spending war in quick commerce seen persisting

The battle for leadership in India’s instant-delivery market is heating up, with Amazon saying its quick delivery business is set to hit annual sales of $1 billion. Zepto’s decision to push back its IPO timeline has lifted shares of rivals such as Eternal and Swiggy. But competition remains intense, with Amazon and Walmart-backed Flipkart continuing to invest in dark stores and accelerate their expansion. For investors, that cuts both ways: the opportunity is big enough to keep attracting deep-pocketed players, but their willingness to spend heavily to gain market share could delay profitability across the industry.

India’s unlisted share market boomed as investors rushed to buy into companies before they went public. But with the National Stock Exchange now set to list, the question is whether investors will stay interested once its main draw is gone. We answer three important questions:
Why was the NSE so important to the unlisted market?

NSE is a large, highly profitable company with a dominant position in its industry and makes regular financial disclosures. Years of delays to its IPO also created an unusually long window for trading its shares. UnlistedZone estimates the bourse alone accounted for roughly half of trading volumes in the market, while its shareholder base swelled to more than 231,000 from fewer than 80 a decade ago.
What happens after NSE lists?

Trading volumes could drop sharply as the unlisted market loses its biggest source of liquidity. Platforms and brokers will need to find new companies capable of attracting investors at a similar scale. That’s tough as few unlisted firms currently offer NSE’s combination of size, profitability, visibility and a clear path to an IPO.
Which sectors could attract attention next?

Investors are likely to look for the next IPO hopefuls across sectors like finance, tech, consumer, defense and market infrastructure. But rather than focusing on finding another NSE, interest may be spread across several companies, with the strongest brands, particularly those with clear listing plans, likely to draw the most attention.

items.title: Copper Gains as Treasury Yields Ease Before Fed Rate Decision
body: Copper steadied as traders eyed rising inventories and loosening spreads ahead of the Federal Reserve’s decision later Wednesday on whether to raise interest rates.

Futures rose slightly on the London Metal Exchange, extending a small gain in the previous session. Prices are still down sharply from a record reached last week that was driven by bets on a US tariff-driven supply squeeze.

Traders have spent the year piling copper into US warehouses hoping to benefit from tariffs that would spike domestic prices, but so far the White House has held off on new measures. Meanwhile, stockpiles held in LME-accredited storage facilities outside the country continued to rise this week, diminishing the threat of a supply pinch.

Three-month futures are trading at a premium of $62.53 a ton to copper for immediate delivery, a market structure known as contango that signals ample supply. In previous weeks the reverse formation — backwardation — that indicates a tight market had prevailed.
The Fed is widely expected to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, which is typically a headwind for non-yielding assets like commodities.
Copper was 0.1% higher at $14,097 a ton on the LME at 9:38 a.m. Singapore time. Other metals were mixed, with nickel down 0.7% to the lowest this year.
Singapore iron ore was down 0.1% to $95.35 a ton.

items.title: Trump Has Few Good Options to Slow China's Rise as AI Superpower
body: Even as Donald Trump blasts Anthropic PBC’s Dario Amodei over his call to hit the brakes on AI development, the two agree on the need to prevent China from catching the US. But doing that remains difficult in practice.

In his 3,800-word missive titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei called on policymakers to avoid selling China advanced AI chips, crack down on chip smuggling and prevent “unauthorized distillation by companies in authoritarian countries,” among other steps. He urged democracies to maintain a lead “as large as possible,” echoing language from the Biden administration.

While Trump maintains export controls on the most advanced chips and chipmaking equipment, he’s also been open to selling China semiconductors such as Nvidia Corp.’s H200s, which Beijing has avoided to develop its own sector. So far his administration has refrained from more punitive measures to crack down on chip smuggling in Southeast Asia, and demurred on sanctions or entity-list designations for Chinese companies found to have carried out systematic distillation from US systems.

The main challenge for the US is keeping China at bay without prompting Beijing to further restrict rare earths used in high-tech products like precision-guided missiles and drones. Trump and Xi Jinping reached a truce last year that saw Beijing guarantee flows of rare earths in return for reduced tariffs, a deal likely to be extended next week when the Chinese leader visits the White House.

“Washington has to tread carefully now that Beijing has sharper retaliatory tools, such as export controls on rare earths,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow in the John L. Thornton China Center at Brookings. “Also, the American AI boom relies on many data center components from China.”

China has continuously narrowed the gap with the US on AI despite the restrictions, as Xi pours money into becoming self-sufficient on the entire tech stack. Although China remains behind on chip production, AI models from companies like DeepSeek and Moonshot have reduced the gap with US frontier offerings in capability, often at a fraction of the cost — threatening to pull away market share from Silicon Valley giants Anthropic and OpenAI.

Trump administration officials, US security agencies and American AI developers alike have accused Chinese firms of distilling from US AI models in the past to build their own products. The practice, which can be legitimately deployed by an AI developer that uses its state-of-the-art model to effectively teach a more power-efficient version, is seen as an improper shortcut when done without approval.

US lawmakers are also considering measures aimed at penalizing Chinese companies found to be copying unfairly from their American counterparts. A harder loophole to close is Beijing’s ability to remotely rent America’s best semiconductors at Southeast Asia cloud data centers — especially after Trump alienated many of those countries with last year’s trade war.

Competition is also expanding throughout the world. Huawei Technologies Co., China’s biggest competitor to Nvidia, has bid to build AI data centers for the Egyptian government, drawing alarm and a scramble from Washington to make a counteroffer.

“Both countries see AI as one of, if not the most important arena of strategic competition,” said Daniel Remler, a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security who led AI policy at the State Department under the Biden administration and took part in the first US-China AI dialogue two years ago. “But leaders and senior policymakers on both sides have to see AI in the context of every other issue they have to contend with, from the war in Iran to rare earths.”

The fight to stay ahead is creating fresh tensions as the US government doubles down on accusations that Chinese companies have engaged in “industrial-scale” theft of American AI labs’ intellectual property through a technique known as distillation. Anthropic last week took those accusations a step further by claiming Moonshot AI had routed nearly 300,000 user requests through Claude and passed the results off as its own.

Those issues will be on display when US and Chinese officials sit down for AI talks planned around the Sept. 24 summit between Xi and Trump. AI is also likely to feature prominently in leader talks next week, according to a senior White House official, who said Trump had been in touch with some CEOs to gauge their views on the recent controversy over AI safety.

China has dismissed the recent US claims as groundless, accusing Washington of applying a “double standard” to stifle competition. Beijing has vowed to “resolutely” retaliate against further US actions against Chinese companies.

If the US wants cooperation on AI, China would also like the Trump administration to remove “containment measures” such as export controls and entity-list designations, said Jiang Tianjiao, a research fellow at the Center for Global AI Innovative Governance and associate professor at Fudan University in Shanghai.

“China has always maintained that if you want a dialogue — especially on sensitive technical issues — there must first be mutual political trust,” he said. “That means establishing mutual respect without triggering unnecessary friction in bilateral relations.”

China may also be looking to crack down on distillation due to its own national security concerns. On Chinese e-commerce platforms like Taobao, merchants offer account top-ups and pre-made profiles for Claude, routing queries through domestic services that relay requests via overseas proxy servers — an industry dubbed “API transit stations.”

Data leakage and high-profile user activity are drawing scrutiny from Chinese regulators, opening the door to targeted crackdowns as domestic security agencies take a harder line against reliance on foreign AI infrastructure, Lyu Yizhou, a lawyer with Shanghai Qianpeng Law Firm, wrote in an online post this week.

The last time the two governments held talks on AI in May 2024, the US enjoyed a comfortable lead. China was still months away from its “DeepSeek moment,” and hadn’t deployed its rare-earth supply chain as leverage against the Biden administration’s export controls.

Since then, Xi has used rare earths to push Trump to retreat from three-digit tariffs and thwarted a proposed rule that would have dramatically expanded the number of Chinese companies subject to US sanctions.

China increasingly dominates global markets — and supply chains — across swaths of advanced manufacturing, from electric vehicles and clean energy gear to drones. Washington has responded by shutting some Chinese products out of the US on national security grounds, most recently with an effective ban on Chinese humanoid robots and power inverters. Beijing in turn stiffened controls on drone exports and sanctioned US entities.

Things could escalate further. A bipartisan bill is currently pending in Congress, with an aim to curb China’s remote access to Nvidia chips via cloud computing. The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees chip export curbs, is also scrutinizing the loophole.
But implementation may be challenging.

“It would involve some degree of monitoring for data centers across multiple countries, particularly in Southeast Asia as well as Japan,” said Chan at Brookings. “As with any effort to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips, it will be a matter of degrees and effort, not a black-and-white solution.”

items.title: HSBC, ICICI Propel India Finance Hub With FX Loans for Diaspora
body: HSBC Holdings Plc and ICICI Bank Ltd. in GIFT City have emerged as the biggest lenders to India’s vast diaspora under a special foreign-exchange swap program, signaling the financial hub’s growing role in channeling global capital into the country.

The two lenders in Gujarat International Finance Tec-City, known as GIFT City, disbursed a combined $19.3 billion through the central bank’s concessional swap facility for foreign-currency non-resident deposits which ran from June till the end of August, according to data compiled by the hub’s regulatory body, the International Financial Services Centres Authority.

The Reserve Bank of India’s program drew a surge in foreign-currency funding into the country, boosting activity in GIFT City. The success of the banks could encourage other lenders operating from the center to expand their wealth management operations and draw in more money from non-resident Indians.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi is positioning GIFT City as a zone capable of competing with established financial centers such as Singapore or Hong Kong.
Read More: How India Is Using Its Diaspora to Defend the Rupee: Explainer

The RBI‘s special facility spurred activity in the hub, with HSBC disbursing $10.9 billion and ICICI Bank $8.4 billion. Others included Bank of Baroda, State Bank of India and Canara Bank, according to IFSCA. The banks did not reply to emails seeking comment. Twenty lenders in the zone gave out a combined $52.8 billion in loans under RBI’s program, IFSCA said.

The center, in which firms including HSBC, Standard Chartered Plc and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. have built huge businesses, already offers exemptions from certain taxes and regulatory restrictions, boosting its appeal as an international capital raising venue.

India garnered a record $127 billion from its overseas nationals through special programs, surpassing even the most optimistic estimates and giving policymakers a formidable buffer to defend the currency against external pressures. The central bank offered to take on the risk of currency-hedging costs of FCNR deposits, prompting some lenders such as HSBC to provide loans amounting to up to 19 times the original deposit.

“Capitalizing on the success of the foreign-currency non-resident accounts, we expect banks to aggressively expand wealth management and tap the global Indian diaspora through extensive international outreach,” K. Rajaraman, IFSCA’s chairperson said in an interview in GIFT City, located in the western state of Gujarat.

Banking assets in GIFT City are expected to top $150 billion by the end of September from $120 billion as of end-August, he said, adding that non-resident Indians would be be critical to the hub’s growth. The number of depositors at banks in the zone has risen nearly 50% to about 32,000 as of the end of August from end-March, the regulator said. Three years ago, the tally was only roughly 4,000.

Rajaraman said the pace at which existing retail customers are being brought on board in the hub is comparable with financial centers such as Singapore and Hong Kong and takes about two to three days. The due diligence for new customers in GIFT City typically takes 10 to 12 days, though that period is expected to shorten as know-your-customer requirements are being streamlined.
Assisted video KYC is already available to NRIs, while unassisted face authentication via a biometric system is expected to be enabled by the end of 2026, he said.

GIFT City’s infrastructure now enables interbank transfers to be completed within seconds at the center. A simplified tax regime and faster operating infrastructure are also helping the hub compete for international capital, according to Rajaraman.

items.title: Takaichi Projects Power in Cabinet Reshuffle Before US Trip
body: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is poised to keep her core team in place in a customary reshuffle nearly a year after taking office, showing renewed confidence after weathering market turmoil and coalition frictions.

After weeks of speculation, Takaichi on Thursday is expected to retain Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, top diplomat Toshimitsu Motegi and defense chief Shinjiro Koizumi, signaling to financial markets she believes her policies are working. She’s also set to give right-leaning coalition partner Japan Innovation Party, or Ishin, its first ministerial post — cementing the union that sealed her election victory as the main opposition splinters.

The continuity on display contrasts with Japan’s two previous leaders. In 2022, Fumio Kishida changed 14 of his 19 ministers in a dramatic overhaul after public outrage over his party’s ties to a religious group, while Takaichi’s immediate predecessor Shigeru Ishiba resigned around one year into the job. Takaichi’s administration has been relatively free from scandal and her support rates remain firm.

“Heading into 2027, Takaichi’s political standing is very strong,” said David Boling, managing director for Japan at the Asia Group. “She increasingly looks a prime minister with real staying power, closer to Shinzo Abe’s model of dominance than to Ishiba’s brief and failed premiership.”
Achieving her ambitious goals to transform Japan over the next six months will come down to establishing “diehard supporters” within the Liberal Democratic Party, he added.

For Takaichi, who is known for working independently rather than socializing with politicians, her operating style could complicate that task. She’s described getting three hours sleep per night as she pores over government documents, drawing concerns about exhaustion and isolation.

Still, retaining her core cabinet after a year that’s seen Katayama field unprecedented policy demands from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and her diplomats navigate a spat with China, shows Takaichi is on good footing with her top lieutenants. She also kept the ruling party’s senior leadership team intact, solidifying her support base within the party.

The fate of Yoshimasa Hayashi, who battled Takaichi for the LDP leadership last year, has been under a spotlight, although one local media report suggests he could stay as internal affairs minister. Changes to lower profile ministers are also likely in the works.

Takaichi is shoring up power at home before heading next week to New York to potentially meet Donald Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. Demonstrating Japan is a reliable and important ally before the US leader hosts Xi Jinping in Washington will be a key diplomatic goal, after she last year offended Beijing with comments over self-ruled Taiwan.

Takaichi was originally scheduled to address the UN on Sept. 24, the day Trump welcomes Xi for a grand state dinner, according to a previous UN schedule. Japanese officials have since avoided that awkward split screen, with Takaichi now speaking on the Tuesday when Trump is also slated to address the UN although no meeting has yet been publicly announced.

With Trump ramping up pressure on fellow US ally South Korea to send support to the Strait of Hormuz, keeping the US on side is important for Takaichi. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s popularity rating hit a record low this month after suggestions Seoul could help the US over Iran. By contrast, Takaichi’s approval rating currently remains robust at around 53%, according to the latest poll by public broadcaster NHK.

Takaichi has two things going that could please Trump. Japan has been outpacing other nations by announcing two rounds of investment projects in the US worth $109 billion, or roughly 20% of a $550 billion initiative established under a trade deal last year. Japan is also buying more oil from the US as it reduces its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted by the war.

“The biggest challenge for Japan’s foreign policy is managing its relationship with China effectively, but the reality is that Takaichi has completely failed to do so,” said Kensuke Takayasu, professor of political science at Waseda University. “Takaichi’s stance on the China issue is at odds with Trump’s. Trump wants to take a more conciliatory approach.”

Once Takaichi returns from New York, her focus will turn back to parliament, where her policies continue to face reservations from bond investors. The benchmark 10-year note’s yield hit 3% earlier this month for the first time since 1996, driven by concerns over inflation and fiscal plans, as well as expectations the Bank of Japan may need to raise interest rates more quickly.

When parliament restarts in early October, Takaichi needs to persuade lawmakers a planned sales tax cut, higher defense spending and her investment roadmap won’t undermine the finances of the world’s most indebted major economy.
Read more: Japan Eyes Defense Spending at 3.5% of GDP After US Pressure

While Japan’s first female leader secured her country’s largest single-party election victory since World War II in February as voters embraced her direct style, she still has doubters in the LDP where many see her as an outsider. To drive through Japan’s biggest budget on record at ¥143 trillion ($921 billion) and oversee a ¥370 trillion investment plan to enhance Japan’s growth, she’ll need their support.

Her efforts to build a stronger military got a boost this month when a candidate backed by the ruling coalition won the governor’s race in Okinawa prefecture. That builds momentum ahead of hundreds of local votes in April and Takaichi’s own bid to retain the presidency of the ruling party next September.

Takaichi also chose continuity in the LDP’s power structure. On Wednesday, she kept former premier Taro Aso, who leads the party’s only remaining formal faction, as LDP vice president, and Shunichi Suzuki — Aso’s brother-in-law and a former finance minister — as the party’s secretary-general.

“The party and government will work together to overcome difficulties and open a path to the future through our policies until the people feel a sense of prosperity and ease through economic growth,” Takaichi told reporters.

While Takaichi appears well positioned to retain power, pressing ahead with a sweeping conservative agenda — such as revising the nation’s constitution — could damage her political capital. Moves to punish national flag desecration, create a second capital to Tokyo and expand the pool of men eligible to become emperor helped bring her honeymoon period to an end, while discontent over inflation has persisted.
Takaichi remains popular among the Japanese public, said William Chou, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, who sees her bigger challenge as forging connections with lawmakers.
“Her long-term premiership will depend on her policies,” he added. “But also her ability to build a political base in the LDP and, most of all, taking care of her health.”

items.title: New Zealand's World-Beating Sovereign Wealth Fund Returns 14.2%
body: The New Zealand Superannuation Fund, one of the world’s top-performing sovereign wealth funds, returned 14.2% in the year through June, powered by a rally in global equity markets despite being underweight in outperforming tech stocks.

About half of the portfolio is invested in equities while being underweight US stocks, Jo Townsend, chief executive of Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation that oversees the fund, said Wednesday in an interview.

“For us, it’s about the valuations,” Townsend said, adding that US stocks look expensive. Instead, she said the fund has “found other investment opportunities that we believe will add diversification and return benefits to the portfolio over the longer term.”

NZ Super takes a total portfolio approach, a strategy that involves collaboration across the portfolio management team to optimize the whole portfolio rather than individual asset classes. Around 40% is in private markets investments such as property, timberland and private equity, she said. The fund has also been buying bonds while they are cheaper, although it doesn’t amount to a significant asset allocation change, she said.

Townsend was speaking after NZ Super posted its pre-tax return after costs in the latest financial year, with funds under management rising NZ$9.3 billion ($5.4 billion) to NZ$94.4 billion. The fund is still on track to double in size every 10 years, Townsend said, adding that as it gets bigger, investing become a “more challenging” task.

“That’s occupying our mind,” she said. “How do we use AI to improve capability and manage risk in the organization?” She cited “getting ready to manage scale and manage risk in an increasingly volatile environment,” as a key challenge.

The fund, which began investing in 2003, was created by the then-center-left government to help finance the rising cost of the state pension. As a result, there will not be meaningful withdrawals for another 30 years, Townsend said.

Over the 10 years from 2015, the fund’s average annual pre-tax return after costs is 10.3%, making it one of the top-ranked funds tracked by consulting firm Global SWF. Over the past 20 years, it has achieved an annual average return of 9.7%, compared with the reference portfolio’s annual average return of 8.2%.

items.title: Shrinking China Fuel Stockpiles Raise Chance of Export Curbs
body: China’s gasoline and diesel inventories are plunging as refiners grapple with a tightening domestic market, raising the chance the government may move to limit fuel exports again.
Gasoline stockpiles at Chinese state-owned fuel suppliers dropped 2.9% last week to the lowest since 2022, according to JLC International. Diesel holdings declined 2.4% to a 15-month low.

Beijing moved quickly to curb oil product exports in the early weeks of the US-Iran war, depriving Asian buyers of much-needed fuel but also helping to keep a lid on global crude prices. Authorities subsequently eased the restrictions, and shipments of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, known as clean products, had recovered to a combined 2.55 million tons in July, according to the latest Chinese customs data.

“With the domestic market tightening, we see an increasing risk that Beijing could restrict monthly clean product exports to around 1.2 million tons in the fourth quarter,” said Jianan Sun, an analyst at Energy Aspects Ltd. in London.

China’s government strictly controls the amount of fuel refiners can export, and they were only allowed to resume and increase shipments on the condition that they keep inventories at elevated levels.

With some oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz, volumes are still well below pre-war levels. And the recent closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline and Houthi territorial gains in Yemen are threatening shipments via the Red Sea. Chinese independent refiners, meanwhile, have lost access to their favored Iranian crude due to the US blockade.

That’s pushing up premiums for oil from Africa and Latin America, as Chinese buyers scramble to source alternative barrels. The situation is becoming so dire for the independents, or teapots, that they may have to cut run rates in the coming weeks.
JLC, a Chinese industry consultant, collects data directly from oil majors’ provincial marketing companies across the nation. The government doesn’t release official inventory figures.

Xinjiang’s rail expansion will triple outbound coal capacity to almost 300 million tons by 2027, shifting China’s marginal thermal coal pricing toward cheaper inland supply and away from seaborne imports, said Bloomberg Intelligence.

The US and China are discussing slashing tariffs on certain goods, including on American energy and agricultural shipments — a potential sign the leaders’ summit next week will lead to an extension of the one-year trade truce.
China’s top iron and steel industry body has called on domestic mills to rein in production and reduce inventories as oversupply and weak demand weigh on the market.

items.title: Meta's Zuckerberg Favors Evaluators Over Slowdown for AI
body: Meta Platforms Inc. Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said artificial intelligence labs should rely on independent evaluators and advisers to ensure that models are safe.

“Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice,” Zuckerberg wrote Tuesday in a post on X, joining a growing chorus of technology executives weighing in on a global debate over the best way to prevent AI systems from harming humanity.

Some company officials have voiced support for decelerating the pace of AI development and advocated working together to achieve consensus. Meta decided on its own to slow work on the Muse AI tool, rather than ask peers to also check their own progress first, Zuckerberg wrote.

“Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security,” he wrote. “We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”

A turbulent debate over AI’s economic and safety risks accelerated over the weekend with a 3,800-word essay from Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei, who urged a slowdown in the pace of development of the most advanced systems so researchers can better understand potential threats. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk — whose companies are bitter rivals to Anthropic — endorsed Amodei’s missive, and an OpenAI executive said the company was working with Anthropic and Alphabet Inc.’s Google on AI safety.

Zuckerberg’s post marked the CEO’s first public foray into the latest round of discussions about how to address the escalating concerns, adding to comments from executives from across the AI industry and lawmakers worldwide. Earlier Tuesday, Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang made similar remarks, saying safety should be a regular part of the development process, and companies can decide not to release things that are harmful.
“Safety is paramount,” Huang said during a Salesforce Inc. event. “In a lot of ways, it’s job one. However, safety is an engineering problem.”

If we reach a point when “the company is out of control and the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right,” he said. Huang also dismissed the need for new AI security regulations, arguing that market forces will help companies safely innovate.
“We don’t need new laws — we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said. The CEO added that there’s a “false choice” about AI development being either safe or fast.

“You can definitely have both at the same time,” Huang said during a conversation with Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff. “You pace yourself until you’re confident you’re releasing something that the market would appreciate. The market forces are already there.”
Read More: Anthropic, OpenAI Safety Push Risks ‘Regulatory Wall’ for Rivals
At the same Salesforce conference, OpenAI’s Altman likewise struck a calmer note, saying he thinks AI companies can develop the technology safely, without causing significant harm to people.
“I am very confident in our company’s ability — our industry’s ability — to do this safely,” Altman said.
While OpenAI is working with Anthropic and Google’s DeepMind lab to address safety issues, Altman said AI companies should be able to safely improve AI models on their own.
“I’m disappointed by how it’s been framed,” he said.

items.title: Gold Rises as Traders Weigh Oil Decline Before Key Fed Decision
body: Gold was steady after a two-day drop as high oil prices continued to fuel inflation concerns and keep interest-rate hike bets a near-certainty ahead of the Federal Reserve’s policy decision later Wednesday.

Bullion was trading around $4,290 an ounce. Elevated energy prices pushed bond yields higher, and traders are now pricing in a 92% chance of the Fed hiking rates. Higher borrowing costs are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

The 10-year US Treasury yield rose to the highest level in almost two decades, the latest milestone in a bruising global bond selloff driven by booming capital investment and soaring energy prices that are exacerbating inflation. The yield, which serves as a benchmark for borrowing costs across the globe, rose as much as five basis points to 5.04% on Tuesday, the highest since 2007.

That’s adding to investor expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates for the first time since 2023. If it doesn’t, or if Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is noncommittal about additional increases, traders may demand even higher yields on long-term bonds to safeguard their investments against the risk of inflation remaining elevated.
Read More: US 10-Year Yield Rises to Highest Since 2007 as Fed Looms

“With markets already pricing a high chance of a Fed hike this week, the main uncertainty is less about the hike itself, and more about what comes after,” said Christopher Wong, a strategist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. “If the Fed keeps the door open to further tightening, gold may be more vulnerable,” and move lower toward $4,000 an ounce if key support at $4,250 is broken, he added.

Oil steadied after a two-day gain, as the duration of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline shutdown after attacks last week remains unclear. The route had allowed millions of barrels a day to avoid passing through the Strait of Hormuz, and Saudi Aramco is now delaying deliveries to some European customers.

Gold is down more than 3% in September, after trading above $4,700 an ounce in late August, as traders repeatedly recalibrate the outlook for Fed policy. Still, many investors are betting that bullion will regain momentum once it rediscovers its traditional value as a portfolio hedge.

Spot gold was 0.2% lower at $4,284.99 an ounce at 8:45 a.m. in Singapore. Silver was little changed at $63.68 an ounce. Platinum dipped 0.2% and palladium was up 0.1%. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was 0.1% higher after gaining 0.6% in the past two sessions.

items.title: Apollo Gives $585 Million of Financing to The Executive Centre
body: Apollo Global Management has provided $585 million of financing to flexible workspace provider The Executive Centre, according to a statement, in the global asset manager’s largest Asian hybrid deal combining debt and equity.

The Executive Centre, acquired by a KKR & Co. and a Tiga Investments Pte.-led consortium in 2021, operates in 38 cities in 15 markets across the Asia Pacific and the Middle East. Proceeds of the funding will be mainly used to refinance existing debt, according to the statement.

Apollo, like other major global alternative asset managers, is increasing its presence in Asia and the TEC funding follows deals with companies including international school chain Global Schools Group and Charles Monat Associates, an insurance brokerage firm for wealthy clients. The current deal involved a competitive process, and is an example of how the US firm is taking share in the region’s loan market, where many deals are still controlled by banks.
Apollo recently invested $1.5 billion in a fund of Singapore asset manager Keppel Ltd. The fund will hold a portfolio of offshore energy assets.
The US asset manager had over $1 trillion of assets under management at the end of June, according to its website.
